result.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers pick per-teacher tiers at 12 and 30 students, explain why per-lesson and per-student pricing are worse, and give similar prices. B does better on the move-over plan, with a 6-month timeline and what happens to each group, and on how to check the prices: churn thresholds, watching for teachers bunching just under 12, and calls with Pro studios. B has two flaws: it says everyone stays at $9 for 6 months but also that Starter teachers drop to $7 immediately, and its 15%-cancellation cutoff doesn't match its own numbers, since losing 15% of Pro teachers costs far less than the extra $13 each brings in. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers recommend three tiers by active student count with similar prices. A does more of what the rubric asks: it gives a dated, group-by-group plan for moving the existing 900 teachers, checks its revenue and churn maths, and names concrete tests and trigger points for changing course, including clustering just under a tier limit, which is a real downside of tiers. B is solid and is the only one to use the 6-vs-55 comparison directly, but its migration plan is vaguer, it states that big studios are the least likely to switch as if it were fact, and its fallback revenue figure is a little off ($8,595, not about $8,800).
